page.h1: HTS Chapter 52: Cotton — U.S. Exports & Foreign Tariffs

seo.title: Chapter 52 U.S. Cotton Exports: Who Buys & Foreign Tariffs
seo.shortDescription: How much raw cotton, yarn and fabric the U.S. exports, who buys it, and what each top buyer charges, from 2020–2025 UN Comtrade data.

intro:
The U.S. exported **$5.88 billion** of Chapter 52 goods in 2025, down **4.8%** from 2024. **Raw cotton (heading 5201) is 82%** of that and cotton yarn (5204–5207) another **13%**; woven cotton fabric is under 5%. **Viet Nam (22%) and Pakistan (12.7%)** are the two largest buyers, and Viet Nam's purchases more than doubled (**+122%**). The big loss is China, whose purchases fell **85%** to $221 million.

Tariffs are low where the volume is. Viet Nam charges nothing on raw cotton, Mexico, Honduras, the Dominican Republic and Guatemala are free under trade agreements, and the rates for Pakistan, Türkiye and Bangladesh were not confirmed from an official source. China is the exception: it charges a 1% rate inside its import quota and 40% above it, plus an extra 10% on every U.S. good, after lifting its 15% tariff on U.S. cotton on November 10, 2025. India is the swing buyer: its normal 11% duty on cotton was waived from August 2025 and, according to press reports, again in mid-2026, which helped lift its purchases 85%.
valueBasis: FOB value of U.S. exports, as reported by the United States to UN Comtrade.

keyTakeaways: Raw cotton is 82% of this chapter, yarn 13% and fabric under 5%. Viet Nam (22%) and Pakistan (12.7%) take 35%, with Türkiye (11.3%) and Honduras (9.4%) next.
Most large buyers charge little or nothing on raw cotton: Viet Nam 0% (yarn 5%), and Mexico, Honduras and the Dominican Republic duty-free under trade agreements.
China is the outlier: it charges 1% inside its 894,000-tonne quota and 40% above, plus an extra 10% on all U.S. goods, and its purchases of U.S. cotton fell 85% in 2025.
India's cotton import duty (normally about 11%) was waived from August 2025 and, per press reports, again from June to October 2026, so a lapse is the main tariff event for U.S. cotton to watch.
